findings.notes: Produced by the check_count_percent tool, not by hand; recorded under no_tool_exists only because the schema's technique enum has no entry for that tool. 3131/4494 = 69.67%, not the printed 70.00%; the printed figure implies a denominator of about 4473. The denominator itself is internally coherent: 107 participants x 6 surveys per day x 7 days = 4494, so it is built on the analytic sample rather than the 112 enrolled (which would give 4704). The most likely innocent explanation is that 70.00% is the MEAN of participants' individual compliance rates rather than the pooled ratio printed beside it; the two differ whenever compliance varies across participants, and the paper does not say which it reports. A second possibility is presentational rounding of 69.67%. Either way the sentence pairs a count, a denominator and a percentage that do not reconcile, and the exactly-round 70.00% to two decimals is what makes it worth a query rather than a shrug.

findings.title: Table2 direct effect row mislabelled
findings.description: A two-step mediational path cannot by definition appear under 'Direct effects', and the same label appearing twice within one model block with different numbers makes the duplication self-evident. The values themselves are not in question -- the regression check reconciles every one of them -- so this is a labelling defect, not a data defect. It nonetheless mislabels the b-path, which is the single load-bearing coefficient of the paper's mediation argument, and does so identically in all six models, so a reader working from Table 2 alone would misread the paper's central result. Most plausibly a copy-paste of the Indirect-effects row label during table preparation.

findings.description: This is a finding about REPORTING PRECISION, not about the authors' arithmetic. findings.notes: The paper builds a substantive interpretation on this null -- it argues in the Discussion that 'there was greater variability in whether moment-to-moment changes in the two self-regulatory factors promoted this LOC eating outcome' and offers explanations (others entering the room, alternative coping behaviours) for why the pathway is absent. But the data are compatible with an indirect effect up to 0.099, which is LARGER than the three indirect effects the paper reports as significant (0.10, 0.09, 0.09 in Models 1, 4 and 6). findings.title: Supplement s4 boundary significance
findings.description: No discrepancy is alleged: the reported p = .049 lies inside the interval [.047, .056] that the printed b and SE permit, so the check passes. findings.title: Supplement s6 attrition null claim
findings.description: The paper states flatly that 'Participants without sufficient data did not differ from those in the analytic sample on baseline methodological, demographic, or psychopathological factors.' None of this suggests anything improper -- 5 exclusions out of 112 is a good retention rate and the authors were right to check -- but the check cannot bear the weight the Methods sentence puts on it, and the honest statement is that comparability could not be established rather than that it was.
